No one ------ For respondent No.2
parties:
Rakhal Dasi Rajakini
Vs.
Ayesha Khatun Chowdhury and another
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J: This appeal is at the instance of the defendant against whom a decree for specific performance of a contract has been upheld in second appeal-S.A.No.405 of 1979-by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division. The principal question involved in this appeal is whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the Court should have refused specific performance of the contract even if it were valid and lawful. 

 2. Both the plaintiff and the defendant are two ladies. Plaintiff-respondent filed O.C. Suit No. 165 of 1969 in the Second Court of Munsif, Tangail, alleging that a written contract was made between her and the defendant for sale of .24 deicmals out of total .33 decimals of land in Tangail town for a consideration of Tk. 2400/- out of which Taka 1000/- was paid by the plaintiff to the defendant on 14 March 1967 and on that very day a Bainapatra (Ext.1) was executed by the defendant who promised to execute the necessary kabala on receipt of the balance. The balance was offered but it was not accepted by the defendant who, after some prevarication, refused to execute the document and denied the contract altogether. The defence taken by the defendant is that at the relevant time there was a genuine apprehension that her land would be taken over by the Government as an enemy-property under the Defence of Pakistan Rules whereupon she requested the plaintiff's husband, an influential man in the locality, to take necessary steps so as to prevent the land from being declared and taken over as enemy property. Accordingly on the advice of the plaintiff's husband, the defendant put her thumb impression on a blank paper but this blank paper was subsequently converted to a Bainapatra supporting to the alleged contract for the sale of her land. This land constitutes a part of her homestead as well. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the contract; but the lower Appellate Court reversed the finding and held that the contract was proved and accordingly decreed the suit for specific performance of the contract. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in second appeal as referred to did not find any ground to interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the final court of facts namely, the lower Appellate Court. 

 3. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the appellant, has tried to convince us that the finding of the lower Appellate Court is not based upon proper consideration of the evidence on record, particularly the fact that the Bainapatra is itself "deceptive in appearance" and no attesting witness has been examined to prove due execution along with the making of the contract and the payment of the earnest money. But in view of the evidence of four witnesses including P.W.3, scribe of the Bainapatra, who said that he had written the Bainapatra at the instruction of defendant No.1 and that the earnest money was received by her in his presence whereupon she put her thumb impression thereon, this contention as to due execution has been rightly rejected by the lower Appellate Court as well as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division. It is true that the plaintiff's husband took steps with the authorities for preventing the property from being taken over as an enemy property. But this he did at the request and in the interest of the appellant herself. We therefore find no reason to disturb the finding that the appellant entered into a valid contract for sale of the land to the respondent. But the question is whether the specific performance of this contract should be allowed merely because it is lawful to do so. Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act provides that the jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, but the discretion should not be exercised arbitrarily but according to the judicial principles. The section is quoted below: 

 "22. Discretion as to decreeing Specific Performance: The jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the Court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so; but the discretion of the Court is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal". 

 5. In the result, the specific performance is refused but the appellant is directed to refund the earnest money of Tk. 1000/- and also pay solatium of Taka 2,000/- to the respondent, in all Taka 3,000/- within two months from the date, failing which, interest at the rate of 15% will be charged upon this amount till paid. Subject to this direction the appeal is allowed, the impugned decree is set aside and the suit is dismissed.
